analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to offer free online tax filing and, for simple returns, prepare taxes for taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have created a free government alternative to paid tax software, was introduced in April 2019 and died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Treasury Department and the IRS to build and run free online tax preparation and filing software. Taxpayers would be able to download the wage and income information employers and banks already report to the IRS, and people with simple tax situations — wages, interest, or dividends and the standard deduction — could elect to have the IRS itself prepare their return. It also bars the Treasury Secretary from signing any agreement, like the existing one with commercial tax software companies, that restricts the government's right to offer filing services. The bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of taxpayers, especially the roughly one-third of filers with the simplest returns (wages, interest, or dividends and the standard deduction), who could file free and pre-filled instead of paying $30–$200 or more for commercial software or a preparer. Because the bill also moves wage-reporting deadlines earlier, the IRS would have taxpayers' income data in hand weeks sooner, making auto-prepared returns possible.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to operate free online tax preparation and filing software by January 31, 2021, with no fee to any participating taxpayer.
Lets taxpayers download their third-party-reported income information (wages, interest, dividends) from the IRS website, so a pre-filled return no longer has to be reconstructed by hand or paid for.

Creates a program letting single, standard-deduction filers with only wage, interest, and dividend income elect to have the IRS prepare their return, with eligibility expandable to married couples, heads of household, and EITC and child tax credit filers after 2020.

Prohibits the Treasury Secretary from entering any agreement that restricts the government's legal right to provide tax preparation or filing services, targeting the arrangement under which the IRS had pledged not to compete with commercial software.
Moves employer wage-reporting deadlines to mid-February and bars extensions on information returns so the IRS receives income data early enough to pre-fill returns the same filing season.

Prohibits knowledge-based identity verification — the quiz-style checks supplied through credit reporting agencies — for anyone using the new programs, a response to the fraud and data-sales concerns tied to those services.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies would lose revenue from simple-return filers, and credit reporting agencies would lose the identity-verification contracts the bill bans. The IRS would bear the cost of building and running the new systems, funded by appropriations for fiscal years 2020–2024.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax software companies and the IRS's budget

drawbacks.text: Building and operating government filing software and an IRS-prepared-return program would require new appropriations and a significant IRS technology effort, at a time when the agency's funding has been squeezed for years.

The auto-prepared return program is limited at first to single filers with only wages, interest, and dividends who take the standard deduction, so most taxpayers — including many low-income EITC claimants with dependents — would not qualify until the Secretary chooses to expand eligibility.
Eliminating extensions on information returns and requiring earlier wage reporting would give employers and payers less time to compile and submit their data.
Taxpayers remain fully responsible for the accuracy of any return, even one prepared by the IRS, so an auto-prepared return could still contain errors the taxpayer must catch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and widespread: free or pre-filled filing for tens of millions of Americans who now pay for software or preparers, or spend hours reconstructing income data the government already has. The main costs fall on tax software companies and on the IRS's technology budget. The design is cautious — the auto-prepared return starts narrow — but the free software and data-download programs would benefit most filers regardless.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2019, and the committee never scheduled it for a markup or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, with 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats and Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent).
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee held no markup, reported no version, and the full Senate never voted on it during the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial tax preparation and software companies, which kept their paying customer base, and credit reporting agencies, which kept their IRS identity-verification contracts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax software companies and credit bureaus

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Filing Simplification Act of 2019 in the Senate.

for.name: Senate Democratic and Independent cosponsors
for.role: 11 cosponsors (Sens. Shaheen, Whitehouse, Baldwin, Udall, Markey, Duckworth, Hassan, Merkley, Booker, Blumenthal, and Sanders)

against.name: Chair Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; it sat in committee from April 2019 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Commercial tax preparation and software industry (Intuit, H&R Block)
against.role: Tax software and tax preparation companies
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for years against government-run free filing and return-free filing, defending the Free File arrangement under which the IRS agreed not to compete with commercial software.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's sole Independent; the Republican-led Finance Committee never took the bill up, so no bipartisan support for action materialized.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and software companies (Intuit/TurboTax, H&R Block)
industries.note: Free, pre-filled government filing would directly compete with the paid software and preparer products these companies sell to simple-return filers, their core mass market. The bill also bans the no-competition agreement the industry had negotiated with the IRS.

The bill prohibits knowledge-based identity verification — quiz-style checks these agencies supply to the IRS through service contracts — for the new free filing programs, eliminating that line of business in this context.

industries.industry: Commercial tax preparers and paid software users' alternatives
industries.note: Taxpayers who currently pay for filing, and volunteer free-file programs hampered by eligibility limits, would gain a free, no-strings government option.
